idiom_name: class delegation with the by-clause (`class Wrapper(b: Base) : Base by b`)
implementation_notes: Kotlin is the clearest case of the pattern absorbed into the language: the `by` clause after a supertype tells the compiler to store the delegate and generate every member of that interface as a forwarder, and members you declare yourself override the generated ones. Its documentation presents this as the alternative to implementation inheritance with zero boilerplate, so it is the default whenever a class would otherwise implement an interface by delegating; hand-write forwarding only when the forward must be conditional or the delegate must be swapped. Delegated properties (`var x by Delegate()`) are the sibling mechanism for property-level delegation, forwarding `getValue`/`setValue` rather than interface members.
pitfalls: Members overridden in the wrapper are not called from the delegate's own implementations: the delegate can only see its own implementations of the interface, so an override does not change behaviour inside the delegate.

The delegate expression is evaluated once, when the object is constructed: `class D(mut: I) : I by mut` keeps the object that was current then, so reassigning the property afterwards has no effect on the forwarding.
`by` forwards the whole interface (no narrowing) and generates a private field you cannot reach; extension functions and members outside the interface are never delegated.
